claim: Open-source roof snow-load monitor: Swiss snow data in, % of design load and alerts out.
data_label: open data: MeteoSwiss SwissMetNet daily, 5 stations, winters 2017/18, 2018/19, 2020/21
limit: Not validated against measured snow water equivalent, and no real roof sensor was used.
alt: Dark chart of estimated flat-roof snow load in kN per square metre across one winter, with a dashed design-load line and shaded alert bands at 50, 70 and 90 percent of design. A shaded range shows the spread between density models.
post:
A flat-roof hall can carry far more snow than the depth on the ground suggests, and nobody sees the number until something creaks.

I built roof-snow-load-estimator, an open-source Python tool that turns open Swiss snow-station data into a roof load in kN/m2, compares it with a design load, and raises alerts at 50, 70 and 90 percent with hysteresis and a recommended action. It includes a density model for snow depth to water equivalent, rain-on-snow, an altitude transfer from station to site, and an optional MQTT input for an on-roof load cell.

Run on MeteoSwiss daily data for five stations from 990 to 1980 m over three winters, the default model puts the Ulrichen roof at 96 percent of the altitude-formula design load in winter 2017/18, with 68 days above 70 percent. The biggest finding is uncertainty: the peak load differs by a factor of 2.1 depending on which density model you pick, so I show the range instead of one line.

What is not verified: I had no measured snow water equivalent to validate against, no real roof sensor was used, and the design load uses a location offset the user has to supply.

If you manage roofs, would you trust an estimate with a visible uncertainty band, or only a sensor on the roof?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/roof-snow-load-estimator
